behavior: Original Datum System allocator wrapper records requested Rust layout bytes and prefix alignment/header bytes separately. Allocated blocks retain an Arc to their stable scope owner through realloc and deallocation on any thread; no dependency private layout is read.

Synchronous nested scope restoration survives unwinding. Scope creation and observation allocate outside tracked domains to avoid ownership cycles and recursive observation. Failed layout/reallocation leaves original ownership intact.

Default native font creation and text preparation are scoped; shared catalog and measurement scopes are separate. Private capacities remain observable after the scope handle closes until the last allocated block frees. Owner ID matches each renderer local report to process observation.

Reports explicitly include allocator_installed. Reusable renderer-library consumers without the executable allocator cannot treat zero counters as a passing result. Logical public cache reports overlap these allocation scopes and must not be summed.

limits: This changes the native executable allocator wrapper. Unscoped allocations also carry a prefix; per-scope tracking_bytes does not claim all process tracking metadata. Runtime overhead, allocator slack, native malloc/mappings, driver memory and RSS remain separate and unqualified.

Scopes cover Rust allocations made synchronously at the stated boundaries, including owned output/cache and some library metadata. They are not an exclusive private-field decomposition, automatic background-thread attribution, complete per-allocation event history or host-incidence qualification.

Complete per-resource admission/classification, active-frame/private scratch caps, staging/chunking and aggregate CPU/GPU caps remain required atS4. This validates a lifetime-aware method; it does not close full ACC/MEM predicates or S4/S5.
No dependency, vendor, registry-source modification, unsafe dependency-layout inference, prototype/font/budget/resize amendment. No performance or global adoption acceptance.

Counts describe allocator calls that actually occur; optimized-away allocations need no heap accounting. Counter values are never an unsafe correctness precondition. No allocator hook callback uses registry mutexes or formatting; scope control/observation is outside callbacks.
